primary_topics: Keynote address at a UP forum dissecting Gamboa v. Teves (June 28, 2011), August 5, 2011 -- formal disclosure that CJP has been on the PLDT Board of Advisers since mid-2009

Three concerns about the Gamboa decision: (1) due process -- PLDT not a respondent but directed to comply; DOJ and SEC interpretations for 75 years were never challenged; good-faith investors not heard; (2) constitutionalism -- courts should defer to the executive on economic matters; (3) retroactivity -- threatening sanction on investors who relied in good faith on government representations for 75 years is 'most cruel and unfair'

CJP's proposed remedies: (a) give investors a reasonable period (a few years) to comply if the decision cannot be reversed; (b) Congress should pass a law governing an orderly and fair divestment process

The governing legal philosophy: strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation for economic matters -- the judiciary does not have the mandate or expertise to decide on matters relating to the economy
sub_topics: Formal disclosure: 'Inasmuch as this case involves PLDT, let me at the outset formally disclose that I have been sitting as an independent member of the board of advisers of PLDT since mid-2009. That was well after I had retired from the Supreme Court in 2006. In that independent capacity, I do not represent PLDT's management or any stockholder. I cannot propose or second motions in the board of directors. Neither can I vote.'

Gamboa ratio: Justice Carpio's ponencia (9 other justices concurring); capital in Section 11 Article XII = shares entitled to vote in director elections = common shares only; NOT total outstanding capital stock including non-voting preferred shares; SEC directed to apply this definition to PLDT and impose sanctions if in violation

Due process concern 1 -- PLDT not a respondent: 'neither the SEC nor PLDT was a respondent in the case as a corporate entity'; the decision directed the SEC to investigate and sanction PLDT without PLDT having been heard

Due process concern 2 -- 75-year government representation: 'prior to this decision, the government, notably the Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission, have since 1935 uniformly held that the entire capital stock... shall be used in determining the 40 percent allocation'; government used this interpretation in road shows abroad to attract foreign investors; 'Relying on this representation, many foreigners invested in Philippine companies, including public utilities'

Themistocles principle: 'The most basic concept of due process is traced to Themistocles who cried, Strike, but hear me first! One may even agree with the Supreme Court's restriction on foreign stockholdings, but no one, not even the highest court of the land, may impose it without first hearing the persons who would be most adversely affected, the foreign investors.'

Deferential interpretation: 'in construing the economic provisions of the Constitution, courts should, absent grave abuse of discretion, defer to the government, especially the Executive Department'; 'the judiciary does not have the mandate, not to say the expertise, to decide on matters relating to the economy and prosperity'

Retroactive sanction critique: 'Most objectionable is the threat of sanction that the Court ordered the SEC chair to impose retroactively. How can we punish investors who relied in good faith on government's representations over the last 75 years? That is most cruel and unfair.'

Proposed remedies: (1) give investors a reasonable period (a few years) to comply with the new ruling; (2) Congress should consider a new law governing an orderly and fair divestment process that will not unduly derail the country's economic progress

stances.claim: Gamboa v. Teves has a fundamental due process defect: it directs the SEC to investigate and sanction PLDT -- a corporation that was not a respondent in the case and was not heard before the decision. The Themistocles principle ('Strike, but hear me first!') applies: even if the Supreme Court's interpretation of 'capital' is correct, it cannot impose sanctions on investors who relied in good faith on the government's own contrary representations for 75 years without first hearing them.
stances.rhetorical_move: Themistocles-due-process argument: the most basic procedural right (hear me first) as the constitutional defect in the Gamboa sanction directive
stances.confidence: asserted as a firm constitutional position

stances.claim: Retroactive application of the Gamboa ruling to sanction investors who relied in good faith on the DOJ/SEC's 75-year interpretation is 'most cruel and unfair.' The proposed remedy -- a few years for orderly compliance and a new Congress divestment law -- is the constitutionally and economically sound alternative to retroactive punishment.
stances.rhetorical_move: good-faith-reliance-protection argument: investors who trusted 75 years of government representation deserve prospective treatment, not retroactive sanctions
stances.confidence: asserted as both a legal and economic argument

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered August 5, 2011 as the keynote address at a UP forum on Gamboa v. Teves (GR No. 176579, June 28, 2011) -- organized by Professor Florin T. Hilbay of the UP Institute of Government and Law Reform -- this address by CJP opens with a formal disclosure: 'I have been sitting as an independent member of the board of advisers of PLDT since mid-2009... I do not represent PLDT's management or any stockholder. I cannot propose or second motions. Neither can I vote.' He summarizes the Gamboa ratio (Justice Carpio ponente, nine concurring justices): 'capital' in Section 11 Article XII refers only to shares entitled to vote in director elections (common shares), not total outstanding capital stock including non-voting preferred shares; the SEC is directed to investigate PLDT and impose sanctions. CJP raises three concerns: (1) Due process -- PLDT was not a respondent and was not heard; the Themistocles principle ('Strike, but hear me first!') applies regardless of whether the SC's interpretation is correct; (2) Constitutionalism -- 'in construing the economic provisions of the Constitution, courts should, absent grave abuse of discretion, defer to the government... the judiciary does not have the mandate, not to say the expertise, to decide on matters relating to the economy'; and (3) Retroactivity -- since 1935 (75 years), the DOJ and SEC 'uniformly held that the entire capital stock' is used to compute the 40% allocation, and the government used this interpretation in foreign road shows to attract investors; 'how can we punish investors who relied in good faith on government's representations over the last 75 years? That is most cruel and unfair.' His proposed remedies: give investors a few years to comply if the decision cannot be reversed; and Congress should pass a new law governing an orderly and fair divestment process.
